anomaly_def.Name: Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Composite Definition: The database is simultaneously suffering from replication-path backlog (standbys cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL fast enough) and front-end network / connection saturation (clients and internal feeders contend for limited transport and connection resources). The two root causes coexist and interact, producing a compound failure surface that spans both cross-node log shipping and client connectivity.

Combined Phenomena: Administrators observe widening replication-lag and log-position gaps while, at the same time, clients hit connection-establishment timeouts, "too many connections" errors, and elevated round-trip times. Retained WAL segments or relay logs accumulate on the primary, disk usage climbs, and replica read-only queries become increasingly stale. Listener backlog queues fill, half-open or idle sockets linger, and authentication or TLS handshakes stall. Because replication streaming uses the same network and socket infrastructure, packet loss or latency spikes show up as both replay delay on replicas and long client-read / client-write waits on the primary. Failover readiness drops, yet manual switchover attempts may also fail because new replication or monitoring sessions cannot attach.

Causal Chain: Network congestion, firewall inspection, or exhausted server socket slots first throttle throughput for both application sessions and replication streams. Diminished bandwidth causes the replica to fall behind; the primary therefore retains additional WAL segments, increasing disk-I/O pressure and prolonging every subsequent network transfer. The growing backlog lengthens replication sockets’ lifetime, holding server processes and TCP ports open and further depleting connection capacity. Conversely, replication delay pushes read traffic back to the primary when replicas become too stale, inflating client connection demand and amplifying the original network bottleneck. The two anomalies thus reinforce each other in a feedback loop that degrades throughput, inflates latency, and jeopardizes durability and high-availability objectives.

entry.official_definition: Maximum amount of time allowed to complete client authentication; if not completed in time, the server closes the connection.
entry.trigger_condition: A would-be client does not complete the authentication protocol within authentication_timeout.
entry.workload_impact: The server closes the connection attempt, preventing hung clients from occupying a connection indefinitely.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
